heading: `max_expired_per_tick` — a derived compile-time bound
text:
### `max_expired_per_tick` — a derived compile-time bound [LDTL.7.1]

`expired_max` is not a free deployment parameter — it is derivable
from values the compiler already knows:

$\mathit{max\_expired\_per\_tick} = \left\lceil \dfrac{N_{\max} \cdot \Delta_{\mathit{tick}}}{d_{\min}} \right\rceil$

where $N_{\max}$ is the declared maximum working-memory size (a deployment
parameter), $\Delta_{\mathit{tick}}$ the interval between TTL ticks (an
integration parameter, declared alongside $N_{\max}$), and $d_{\min}$ the
shortest TTL among the program's `ttl`-lifecycle schemas (a compile-time
constant from their declarations).

Rationale: in the worst case, all facts have the minimum possible TTL.
At steady state with $N_{\max}$ facts, at most
$N_{\max} \cdot \Delta_{\mathit{tick}} / d_{\min}$ facts accumulate between
ticks.  That many expire on the next tick.  This is the ceiling on expired
facts per tick.

The compiler will carry `max_expired_per_tick` in the artefact's realtime
contract ([RTCT.6]) beside its other bounds, and the engine will check the TTL
queues' capacity against it at the transition to LIVE.

For example, with $N_{\max} = 10{,}000$, $\Delta_{\mathit{tick}} = 100$ ms and
$d_{\min} = 30$ s, `max_expired_per_tick` $= \lceil 10{,}000 \times 0.1 / 30 \rceil = 34$.
Not proportional to $N_{\max}$ in the large-$N_{\max}$ limit; proportional
to $\Delta_{\mathit{tick}} / d_{\min}$, which is a deployment design choice.
